title: KV Cache Compaction Improvements — Design Review (Runtime 1.22)
content:
Slide 1 — Title
KV Cache Compaction Improvements (Runtime 1.22)
Design Review
Owners: Omar El-Sayed (KV cache), Samir Qureshi (allocator/compaction), Sofia Ivanova (scheduler)
Reviewers: Noah Patel (correctness), Allison Grant (metrics), Sean Gallagher (SRE)

Speaker notes:
- Problem statement: burst-driven p95/p99 spikes and intermittent OOM/request shedding correlated with KV arena fragmentation.
- Goal: keep KV memory contiguous/predictable under mixed sequence lengths + churn.


Slide 2 — Why now / customer impact
- Hosted: tail latency spikes under burst traffic; impacts latency commitments + app retries
- Dedicated: customers run long-lived chats + batch jobs together; fragmentation + churn amplifies p99
- Support: recent tickets point to allocator fragmentation patterns (SUP-28411, SUP-28433, SUP-28472)

Speaker notes:
- We can’t “just add GPUs” to fix p99; fragmentation creates non-linear failure modes.
- Prior mitigations (lower max_ctx, conservative admission control, aggressive evictions) trade away quality/throughput.


Slide 3 — Symptoms observed in prod-like runs
- Long-lived sequences hold scattered KV pages (holes accumulate)
- Cancellation + retries increase churn in the free list
- Under burst: allocator spends time searching/defragmenting opportunistically
- Worst-case: OOM due to inability to satisfy large contiguous allocation even with sufficient free bytes

Speaker notes:
- We see p99 spikes clustered with allocator “slow path” hits + background reclaim.
- When we’re close to the edge, evictions happen at bad times (during decode bursts).


Slide 4 — Quick primer: current KV allocation model (today)
- KV arena = pages/blocks allocated per (model, gpu, pool)
- Sequences allocate KV pages as they decode (grows over time)
- Free list returns pages on sequence end/cancel
- Prefix cache uses separate tracking but competes for the same physical arena in practice

Speaker notes:
- The key property: decode is continuous; allocations happen at fine granularity.
- Current allocator is optimized for throughput on the common path, but does not actively manage fragmentation.


Slide 5 — Problem definition: fragmentation
Definitions used in this review (aligned w/ metrics draft):
- Total free bytes: sum of all free pages
- Largest contiguous free run: largest adjacent run of free pages
- Fragmentation ratio (candidate): 1 - (largest_free_run / total_free_bytes)
- “Allocator slow path”: page search + fallback paths that exceed threshold (e.g., N scans)

Speaker notes:
- Ratio isn’t perfect, but tracks our failure mode: inability to satisfy “big-ish” runs for growing sequences.
- We’ll validate metric definitions with Allison/SRE before standardizing.


Slide 6 — Evidence: fragmentation correlates with tail latency
Graph (described):
- X axis: time (10s buckets)
- Left Y: p99 decode latency (ms)
- Right Y: fragmentation ratio
Observation:
- p99 spikes line up with fragmentation rising above ~0.65–0.75 and slow-path allocation count increases

Speaker notes:
- This is from a mixed-length churn workload generator (benchmark-lab/pr-881) configured to mimic Hosted “bursty chat” patterns.
- Correlation is strong but not causal proof; we reproduce in controlled environments with compaction disabled/enabled.


Slide 7 — Design goals / non-goals
Goals
- Reduce fragmentation without harming steady-state throughput
- Reduce burst tail latencies (p95/p99) on mixed length distributions
- Safe + observable + configurable (tier/model/profile)
- Guardrails: budgeted work, backpressure integration, kill-switch

Non-goals (v1)
- Customer UI for tuning (Console)
- Large kernel rewrites unrelated to KV movement (only minimal copy/pack if needed)


Slide 8 — Proposed approach (high level)
1) Make fragmentation measurable + actionable (metrics + thresholds)
2) Add budgeted incremental compaction
   - Move live KV pages to consolidate free runs
   - Work occurs in bounded steps (bytes/time)
3) Add tier-aware eviction policy (separate but integrated trigger path)
   - When we can’t compact fast enough or we’re close to OOM
   - Prefer evicting low-priority / preemptible caches
4) Integrate into scheduler to avoid decode stalls

Speaker notes:
- Core idea: compaction is a “maintenance task” paced by the scheduler so it doesn’t turn into tail latency.


Slide 9 — Compaction mechanism: what actually moves
- Unit of movement: KV page / block (allocator-defined)
- Candidate selection:
  - Find “islands” of live pages that block creating a large free run
  - Avoid moving pages for sequences in critical decode phase (configurable)
- Relocation steps:
  - Allocate destination run
  - Copy page(s) (GPU copy kernel; async where possible)
  - Update sequence’s page table / indirection
  - Free old page(s)

Speaker notes:
- Indirection update is the correctness-critical boundary.
- Cancellation mid-relocation is a known edge case; we added a fix + test plan (see pr-19440).


Slide 10 — Budgeting: why and where enforced
- Budget dimensions (configurable):
  - Bytes moved per window (e.g., 256MB / 1s)
  - Time spent per scheduler boundary (e.g., 0.5–2.0ms)
  - Max relocations per step
- Enforced at scheduler boundaries
  - Option A: prefill/decode boundary hook (preferred)
  - Option B: background worker only (risk: steals GPU during decode)

Speaker notes:
- We want deterministic latency: enforce “small bites” at known safe points.
- In practice we’ll do both: scheduler-driven budget + low-priority background only when the GPU is not saturated (v1 may ship without background).


Slide 11 — Scheduler integration: where compaction runs
- Hook points in serving loop:
  - After prefill completion (before decode starts)
  - Between decode iterations (only if queue pressure is low)
  - During “idle gaps” when batch is under-filled
- Avoid running compaction when:
  - Decode queue is above pressure threshold
  - p99 latency guardrail breached
  - Eviction is actively happening

Speaker notes:
- Sofia’s point: decode is the sensitive phase; running copies at the wrong time increases tail.
- Compaction must be self-throttling with backpressure.


Slide 12 — Eviction policy (tier-aware LRU)
- Eviction is not the first lever; it’s safety under pressure
- Candidate order (draft):
  1) Preemptible prefix cache segments (if allowed)
  2) Low-priority tier sequences (Hosted free/dev tiers) via LRU-by-last-token
  3) Dedicated burst buffers (if configured as preemptible)
- Never evict:
  - Pinned sessions (explicit)
  - System-critical routes
  - Sequences that would violate correctness invariants

Speaker notes:
- We’ll keep the policy simple and explainable.
- Eviction is integrated with routing/backpressure so we can shed load intentionally rather than failing unpredictably.


Slide 13 — Correctness & safety invariants
- Relocation invariants:
  - A KV page is owned by exactly one sequence at a time
  - Page table update is atomic at the sequence abstraction level
  - No read-after-free during decode
- Concurrency hazards addressed:
  - Cancellation while relocating (fixed in pr-19440; additional stress tests planned)
  - Concurrent streaming + sequence teardown
  - Partial batch failures
- Kill-switch:
  - Disable compaction (stop moving)
  - Optionally disable eviction policy
  - Must be safe to flip during incident

Speaker notes:
- Noah’s ask: explicit “stop the world” is unacceptable; kill-switch must degrade safely (compaction stops, allocator returns to old behavior, and we lean on admission control).


Slide 14 — Observability plan (what we’ll ship)
Metrics (draft names; subject to standardization)
- kv_fragmentation_ratio{model,pool,tier}
- kv_largest_free_run_bytes{model,pool}
- kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total{model,pool}
- kv_compaction_time_ms{model,pool,phase}
- kv_evictions_total{model,pool,tier,reason}
- kv_allocator_slowpath_total{model,pool,reason}
Tracing
- Span: kv.compaction.step (bytes_moved, pages_moved, time_ms)
- Span: kv.eviction (count, tier, reason)

Speaker notes:
- We need exemplars to correlate compaction steps with p99 spikes (pr-19405 adds spans).
- SRE wants per-route and per-tier breakdown for canary cohorts.


Slide 15 — Dashboard / alerting (SRE requirements)
Required panels (initial)
- Fragmentation ratio over time, by pool/model
- p95/p99 decode latency overlayed with bytes moved
- Eviction rate + top eviction reasons
- Allocator slow path count
- OOM / request shedding counters
Alert sketch (canary)
- If p99 increases > X% AND compaction_time_ms rises OR bytes_moved spikes => page runtime oncall
- If eviction rate exceeds threshold on paid tiers => rollback gate

Speaker notes:
- Final thresholds to be tuned during canary (see eng-sre alert tuning notes).
- We want automatic rollback conditions for Hosted cohorts.


Slide 16 — Benchmark plan
Workloads
- Mixed prompt/response lengths (heavy tail)
- Burst traffic: step function + sawtooth
- Long-lived sessions + churn (cancellations/retries)
- Prefix cache on/off
KPIs
- p95/p99 decode latency
- Throughput (tokens/s) at fixed cost
- Fragmentation ratio over time
- Bytes moved / compaction overhead
Regression gates
- No >1–2% steady-state throughput loss (model-dependent)
- No sustained p99 increase under steady load

Speaker notes:
- Rina + Marcus will integrate into perf-canary scenario (perf-canary/pr-412).


Slide 17 — Early results (staging bench, draft)
Table (described):
- Model A (7B), A10: fragmentation steady-state 0.78 -> 0.41; p99 decode -18%; throughput -0.6%
- Model B (13B), L4: fragmentation 0.72 -> 0.46; p99 decode -9%; throughput -1.1%
- Model C (70B), H100: fragmentation 0.66 -> 0.44; p99 decode -6%; throughput -0.3%

Caveats
- These are pre-eviction (compaction only)
- Budget defaults still changing (bytes/time)

Speaker notes:
- Biggest wins are on smaller GPUs where memory pressure is higher and allocation behavior is more constrained.
- On H100 the main benefit is stability (less variance) rather than dramatic improvement.


Slide 18 — Tradeoffs / risks
Risks
- Compaction copy overhead steals GPU time
- Bad scheduling placement causes decode stalls (tail regression)
- Correctness bugs in relocation under cancellation/concurrency
- Eviction surprises (customer perception) if it hits paid tiers
Mitigations
- Strict budget + scheduler gating
- Feature flag + staged rollout + kill-switch
- Stress test suite for adversarial churn
- Tier-aware eviction with conservative defaults

Speaker notes:
- We should treat this like a “memory management subsystem change” (high risk) not just a perf tweak.


Slide 19 — Configuration knobs (internal-only v1)
Flags (names illustrative)
- kv_compaction_enabled: true/false
- kv_compaction_trigger_fragmentation_ratio: e.g., 0.60
- kv_compaction_budget_bytes_per_sec: e.g., 256MB
- kv_compaction_budget_ms_per_scheduler_step: e.g., 1.0ms
- kv_eviction_enabled: true/false
- kv_eviction_tier_policy: hosted_free_only | tier_aware
- kv_compaction_max_inflight_relocations: e.g., 4

Speaker notes:
- Config propagation latency matters for kill-switch; we’re coordinating with platform (see eng-platform thread).


Slide 20 — Rollout plan (phased)
Phase 0: internal canary
- Runtime team pools only
- Validate metrics + no correctness regressions
Phase 1: Hosted small cohort
- One region, limited routes/models
- Automated rollback gates (p99 + eviction on paid)
Phase 2: Expand Hosted + Dedicated opt-in
- Dedicated pools with explicit “preemptible eviction” disabled by default
Phase 3: Default-on (case-by-case)
- After 2+ weeks stability + support confirms improvement in known escalation patterns

Speaker notes:
- Rollback must be fast: disable compaction first; if still bad, revert runtime build.
- Ensure release train alignment with Connor (runtime-1.22).


Slide 21 — Open questions
- What is the best fragmentation trigger metric?
  - ratio vs largest_free_run_bytes vs slowpath rate
- Background compaction: do we ship in v1 or wait?
- Prefix cache interaction: do we compact across prefix segments or treat separately?
- How aggressively do we permit compaction during decode under low pressure?

Speaker notes:
- Need a decision by end of week to keep 1.22 timeline.


Slide 22 — Q&A notes (from review meeting)
Q: “What prevents compaction from becoming the new p99 spike?” (Sean)
- A: Scheduler-enforced budget; if queue pressure high, compaction stops. Alert/rollback if compaction_time_ms correlates with p99.

Q: “What’s the correctness proof boundary?” (Noah)
- A: Atomic update of per-sequence page table; relocation is two-phase (copy then swap) with cancellation-safe cleanup.

Q: “Will eviction impact paying customers?” (Nikhil/Lauren)
- A: Default: eviction restricted to preemptible caches + low-priority tiers; Dedicated and paid tiers require explicit enablement.

Q: “Do we need new kernels?” (Hiro/Grace)
- A: Likely minimal: fast contiguous copy/pack paths; start with existing memcpy primitives; optimize only if profiling shows.

Q: “How do we debug incidents?” (Rafael)
- A: Runbook will include: verify flags, check fragmentation panels, check bytes_moved and eviction counters, flip kill-switch, capture allocator snapshot.


Slide 23 — Next steps / owners
- Finalize metric definitions + dashboards (Allison + Logan + Sean)
- Land allocator + compaction core behind flag (Samir, PR series)
- Scheduler budget hook + backpressure gating (Sofia)
- Eviction policy implementation + tests (Omar)
- Stress/conformance suite (Anika + Marcus)
- Canary plan + rollout checklist (Rafael + Talia)

Speaker notes:
- Target: feature complete by end of implementation window; canary start immediately after.


Appendix A — References
- Linear epic: ENG-4821
- Metrics PR: redwood/pr-19342
- Allocator changes PR: redwood/pr-19357
- Scheduler integration PR: redwood/pr-19371
- Eviction policy PR: redwood/pr-19388
- Tracing spans PR: redwood/pr-19405
- Kill-switch plumbing PR: redwood/pr-19422
- Cancellation edge-case fix: redwood/pr-19440
- Workload generator: benchmark-lab/pr-881
- Canary scenario: perf-canary/pr-412

Appendix B — “Graph descriptions” (for text export)
1) Fragmentation vs p99 timeline: shows fragmentation crossing ~0.7 before p99 bursts.
2) Bytes moved histogram: compaction typically moves 64–128MB/min at default budgets; outliers correspond to burst recovery.
3) Throughput scatter: tokens/s unchanged within noise when compaction is throttled; regression appears only when budget >3ms/step.

Notes to self (Omar):
- Add one slide for ‘what happens when compaction can’t keep up’ (eviction + admission control flow) before final share.
- Confirm whether we want to expose “largest_free_run_bytes” as a first-class SLI for allocator health.
